implementation_notes: Core Data's NSManagedObjectContext is the pattern almost verbatim: the documentation calls it an object space to manipulate and track changes to managed objects, exposes insertedObjects, updatedObjects and deletedObjects, and save() commits those changes to the persistent store - changes stay in memory until then. A context is confined to one thread or serialised queue and is reached through perform/performAndWait, so the unit of work doubles as the concurrency boundary, and parent/child contexts commit one store up. SwiftData's ModelContext is the same role for the newer stack: insert/delete, changedModelsArray, hasChanges, save(), rollback() and transaction(block:), with autosaveEnabled controlling implicit saves. Both replace the register/flush structure entirely - you mutate models and save the context.
code_sketch:
let ctx = container.newBackgroundContext()      // unit of work + its own queue
ctx.perform {
    let p = ctx.object(with: objectID) as! Person
    p.email = "new@example.com"                  // appears in ctx.updatedObjects
    ctx.insert(Log(person: p))                   // appears in ctx.insertedObjects
    try? ctx.save()                              // one atomic flush to the store
}
pitfalls: A context is thread/queue-confined: touching managed objects outside its queue is undefined behaviour, and contexts must be created on the queue that will use them.
Changes are committed only one store up - a child context's save() does not reach the persistent store until the root context is saved.
A context that is never saved keeps changes in memory and shows stale values to other contexts; merge policies decide what happens on conflict.
Subclassing NSManagedObjectContext is discouraged because the change-tracking and undo machinery is delicate, so extension must happen through notifications or custom merge policies.

variants.name: SwiftData ModelContext with save()/transaction(block:)
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftData's ModelContext is the unit of work for the newer Apple stack: it tracks the models it fetched or inserted, exposes hasChanges and changedModelsArray, saves explicitly with save() or runs a block with transaction(block:) that writes pending inserts, changes and deletes on completion, and rollback() discards pending work and restores changed models to their last saved state. The SwiftUI environment provides a main-actor context with autosave enabled, so explicit save() is only needed when you want the boundary under your control.
pitfalls: autosaveEnabled on the environment context saves at framework-chosen moments, so a business operation that must be atomic needs transaction(block:) or an explicit save.
The environment context is bound to the main actor; background work needs its own ModelContext on the right actor.
